Basket
BAS-ket
n. (rendering Hebrew sal/tene', Greek kophinos/spuris)
Of uncertain origin, perhaps British. Hebrew has several: sal, the woven basket of the consecration offerings; tene', the basket of firstfruits carried to the sanctuary; kelub, a cage or fruit basket. Greek distinguishes kophinos, the small hand basket a Jew carried on a journey, from spuris, a large hamper big enough to hold a man.

Biblical Definition

Baskets in Scripture carry what is given to God, what God gives back, and occasionally a man. The firstfruits went up in one: “thou shalt take of the first of all the fruit of the earth... and shalt put it in a basket, and shalt go unto the place which the LORD thy God shall choose” (Deuteronomy 26:2) — the confession of faith that follows it is one of the oldest in the Bible. The consecration of Aaron used another: “thou shalt put them into one basket, and bring them in the basket” (Exodus 29:3). After the feeding of the five thousand the arithmetic is deliberately preserved: “they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full” (Matthew 14:20) — twelve kophinoi, one apparently for each disciple who had said it could not be done. Amos is shown one as a pun on the end of a nation: “behold a basket of summer fruit” (Amos 8:1), ripe and about to spoil. And Paul's first exploit as a Christian is an undignified escape: “then the disciples took him by night, and let him down by the wall in a basket” (Acts 9:25) — the great apostle's ministry begins with him being lowered out of a city in a hamper, a detail he later cites as something to glory in.

Webster 1828 Definition

A vessel made of twigs, rushes, or splints interwoven. In Scripture, the basket of firstfruits carried to the sanctuary, the basket of the consecration offerings, the twelve baskets of fragments after the feeding of the five thousand, the basket of summer fruit shown to Amos, and the basket in which Paul was let down the wall.

expand to see more

BASKET, n. 1. A domestic vessel made of twigs, rushes, splinters or other flexible things interwoven.

2. The contents of a basket; as much as a basket will contain.

3. In Scripture, baskets were used for carrying fruit, bread, and the offerings of the sanctuary.

4. Of uncertain origin; perhaps of British derivation.

5. In Scripture, put it in a basket, Deut. 26; they took up twelve baskets full, Matt. 14.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 26:2 — "That thou shalt take of the first of all the fruit of the earth, which thou shalt bring of thy land that the LORD thy God giveth thee, and shalt put it in a basket, and shalt go unto the place which the LORD thy God shall choose to place his name there."

Exodus 29:3 — "And thou shalt put them into one basket, and bring them in the basket, with the bullock and the two rams."

Matthew 14:20 — "And they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full."

Amos 8:1 — "Thus hath the Lord GOD shewed unto me: and behold a basket of summer fruit."

Modern Corruption

The twelve baskets are treated as a pleasant detail rather than as evidence, and the miracle itself is explained away as a lesson in sharing; while firstfruits giving is reduced to a technique for obtaining return.

expand to see more

The standard liberal handling of the feeding of the five thousand is that the real miracle was generosity: a boy shared his lunch, the crowd was shamed into producing hidden provisions, and everyone ate. The account resists it at every point. The disciples state the problem in monetary terms — two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient — and the surplus is the difficulty for the theory, because leftovers do not accumulate when people eat what they brought. Twelve baskets full of fragments after five thousand men, beside women and children, is the evangelists' way of establishing that something was created and not merely distributed. John records the crowd's own conclusion, that this is of a truth that prophet that should come into the world, and their attempt to take Him by force and make Him king — not the reaction of people who had shared sandwiches.

The basket of firstfruits carries a different corruption. Deuteronomy 26 has the worshipper bring the first of the harvest, set it before the altar, and recite what God has done: a Syrian ready to perish was my father, and the LORD brought us out. The giving is a confession, and it is first — before the rest is counted, and therefore before the giver knows whether the year will be good. Prosperity teaching inverts this, presenting the first gift as seed sown for a guaranteed return and turning worship into investment. The principle to recover is the order of the passage: God acted, the worshipper remembers, the basket follows, and the giving is thanksgiving for a redemption already accomplished rather than a deposit against a harvest not yet in.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sal, a woven basket for bread and offerings; tene', the firstfruits basket; kelub, a fruit basket or cage; Greek kophinos, a hand basket, and spuris, a large hamper.

expand to see more

Hebrew sal (H5536) — a woven basket; the basket of unleavened bread at the consecration of the priests (Exodus 29:3).

Hebrew tene' (H2935) — a basket for firstfruits; “shalt put it in a basket” (Deuteronomy 26:2).

Hebrew kelub (H3619) — a cage or fruit basket; the basket of summer fruit shown to Amos (Amos 8:1).

Greek kophinos (G2894) — a small wicker hand basket; the twelve baskets of fragments (Matthew 14:20).

Greek spuris (G4711) — a large hamper; the seven baskets after the four thousand, and the basket that carried Paul (Acts 9:25).

Usage

"Of firstfruits brought with confession: shalt put it in a basket, and shalt go unto the place which the LORD thy God shall choose (Deuteronomy 26:2)."

"Of the surplus that proves the miracle: they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full (Matthew 14:20)."

"Of a nation ripe for judgment: behold a basket of summer fruit (Amos 8:1)."
